routes.description: Establish that contingency, a finite cosmic past, life-permitting fine-tuning, objective morality, and the historical case for Jesus's resurrection collectively raise the probability of God's existence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cited facts are sufficiently established, are more expected or better explained given theism than its relevant alternatives, and cumulatively support the motion's evidentiary threshold.

motionBridge.description: The motion is satisfied if the cumulative considerations make God's existence more probable than it would otherwise be.

centralBridges.description: Contingent reality and a universe with a finite past must warrant inference to a necessary, transcendent causal ground.
Life-permitting constants and initial conditions must be better explained by design than by necessity, chance, or multiverse selection.
Objective moral values and duties must exist and require an ontological foundation supplied by God's necessary moral nature.
The relevant historical facts concerning Jesus must be established and better explained by divine resurrection than by naturalistic alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Philosophical, moral, historical, and scientific considerations must be admissible within a probability-raising conception of evidence.
The several independent considerations must retain material cumulative force even if no individual consideration proves theism by itself.

routes.description: Show that the affirmative considerations are unsupported, underdetermined, or more plausibly addressed through empirical naturalism, so they do not supply adequate evidence for a divine cause or the Christian God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative fails to justify its probability assignments or if natural models, explanatory uncertainty, secular morality, and ordinary historical explanations prevent the cited facts from discriminating in favor of God.

motionBridge.description: The motion is not established unless the affirmative supplies testable or otherwise warranted evidence that favors God over relevant natural alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Quantum-gravity, multiverse, or other physical possibilities must block the inference from contingency or cosmic beginnings to a uniquely divine cause.
Dynamical explanations and observer selection must make apparent fine-tuning insufficient to distinguish purposive design from natural cosmology.
Moral truth or understanding must remain intelligible without divine grounding, or the proposed divine foundation must face an unresolved arbitrariness problem.
Human error, illusion, imagination, or intervention must remain more plausible than resurrection as explanations of the reported historical claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Claims about divine evidence must meet a defensible empirical or probabilistic standard rather than rest on intuition or unquantified priors.
Present explanatory ignorance must remain a reason for continued investigation rather than an evidential inference to supernatural agency.

sections.title: Evidential Standards and the Cumulative Inference
sections.rationale: The parties dispute what qualifies as evidence, how probability-raising claims are warranted, where the burden lies, and whether several distinct considerations can jointly support the motion.

sections.title: Contingency and the Necessary Explanatory Ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether contingent reality requires an external necessary explanation and whether God has any justified advantage over a necessary or eternal natural terminus.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Infinity, and Transcendent Causation
sections.rationale: The finite-past argument depends on philosophical claims about actual infinity, scientific claims about cosmic boundaries, and the inference from a beginning to a transcendent cause.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Multiverse Selection
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether life-permitting conditions favor purposive design or are better treated through dynamics, varied universes, observer selection, and unresolved physical theory.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: The moral argument requires both objective values or duties and a uniquely divine ontology, while the opposing route contests that dependence through rational, biological, and arbitrariness-based alternatives.

sections.title: Resurrection and Competing Historical Explanations
sections.rationale: The historical pillar turns on the status of the alleged facts, their connection to God's existence, and the comparative plausibility of resurrection against ordinary human explanations.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Facts concerning the universe, morality, and history collectively raise the probability that God exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening statement explicitly introduces Craig's probabilistic conception of evidence and cumulative case.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines the probability-raising standard and introduces the cumulative route without answering an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the governing standard and previews the relevant considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative probability claim, its evidence variables, and its cumulative scope are expressly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probability-raising formulation is appropriately limited, though calling its application indisputable outruns the stated support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Bayesian comparative standard is coherent, but the cumulative independence and prior-probability bridges remain compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The formal probability relation is specific, while the promised applications rather than this span supply most substantive warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the motion-level probability condition and organizes every affirmative evidentiary consideration.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own evidentiary standard and does not materially characterize a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly compares the probability of God given evidence and background information with background information alone.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The existence of contingent beings is best explained by a necessarily existing transcendent cause identified as God.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his first consideration and presents both an explanatory inference and its deductive formulation.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative contingency argument and its necessary-cause conclusion without targeting an earlier opponent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives an explicit explanatory principle, applies it to the universe, and states the intended conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contingent-versus-necessary distinction is stable, although the identification of the terminus with God is compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explicit argument supports an explanatory terminus, but the stronger identification with a transcendent God needs another bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference to a necessary explanation is usable, but the move compresses why the necessary terminus is transcendent and divine.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explanatory principle is stated rather than independently defended, and rival necessary natural termini are not compared here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable contingency-to-necessary-ground bridge for the affirmative cosmological route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily states its positive argument and does not substantially interpret an opposing account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span states that contingent beings increase God's probability and gives the premise that existence is explained internally or externally.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent cause beyond space and time, best identified as God.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly presents his second argument, supports its premises, and closes with a numbered deductive formulation.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents the finite-past causal argument and its transcendent-cause conclusion without answering an earlier opponent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it explicitly numbers the causal premises and conclusion and connects them to the theistic inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal syllogism is explicit, while the further move from a cause to God remains an implicit explanatory qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The syllogistic causal conclusion is stronger than the supplied warrant for identifying that cause specifically as God.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated syllogism is valid, but the beginning premise and the bridge from cause to transcendent divine agency require further defense.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A clear argument and referenced cosmological support are supplied, though scientific boundary claims and divine identification remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central requirement that a finite cosmic past warrants a transcendent causal ground.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive presentation does not materially characterize a developed opposing model within the selected evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly states that everything beginning has a cause, that the universe began, and that a transcendent cause follows.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by design than by physical necessity or chance.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig identifies fine-tuning as his third consideration and explicitly compares necessity, chance, and design as explanations.

response.rationale: This constructive move frames necessity, chance, and design as rival explanations and argues affirmatively for design.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly lays out the comparative alternatives and begins eliminating the principal rivals.

precisionFindings.rationale: Fine-tuning and the three proposed explanation classes are clearly distinguished and consistently used.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative inference has support, but the exhaustive three-way framing and relevant probability distributions remain underqualified.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning may result from physical necessity or chance rather than design.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those alternatives require defended probability measures and may include multiverse selection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative structure is coherent, with a bounded gap concerning exhaustiveness and the probability basis for design.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The independence of constants from laws is specifically invoked, but chance measures and multiverse alternatives are not fully assessed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central design-over-necessity-and-chance completion condition for the fine-tuning route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move squarely names necessity and chance, though it does not yet address the strongest observer-selection version of chance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span identifies physical necessity, chance, and design and argues that independent constants are not fixed by natural laws.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, and their existence entails God because atheism cannot ground their objectivity.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his fourth argument and concludes with an explicit three-premise-style deductive presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move asserts objective moral truths and presents their dependence on God as a deductive affirmative argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states both the moral-objectivity premise and the intended theistic consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Objective values and duties are consistently invoked, but the kind of ontological dependence intended is only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Assigning probability 1.0 to God from moral wrongness radically compresses the disputed grounding premise and alternative metaethics.

charity.alternative: Objective moral truths could exist without being constituted or commanded by God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument must establish ontological dependence, not merely moral realism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The deductive form is recoverable, but the central conditional from no God to no objective morality is asserted rather than bridged.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples support belief in objective wrongness, yet they do not establish that only God can ontologically ground that wrongness.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses both required components of the central objective-morality and divine-grounding bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move largely treats atheism as unable to ground objectivity without engaging the strongest secular moral-realist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses an example of categorical moral error and then explicitly begins the conditional argument from objective morality to God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples' transformed belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection, which entails God.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels the historical case his fifth argument, enumerates three facts, and states the resurrection inference and theistic conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces three historical claims and argues that resurrection best explains them and entails divine agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies the relevant facts, the comparative explanatory claim, and the theistic consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-fact structure and resurrection inference are clear, though scholarly agreement and evidential independence are compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative conclusion is intelligible, but the excerpt does not fully qualify dependence among sources or miracle base rates.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory inference is coherent, but the bridge from the three claims to resurrection and then to God remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific alleged facts and broad scholarly recognition are cited, while source independence and natural rivals receive little verification here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the historical facts and best-explanation claim required by the affirmative resurrection bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opening constructive case does not yet develop a specific rival historical explanation sufficiently for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span names the empty tomb and presents three facts said to be recognized by most New Testament historians and explained by resurrection.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Craig bears the affirmative burden of supplying recognizable empirical evidence for God, while Krauss need not disprove God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss explicitly distinguishes this evidence debate from a general existence debate and repeatedly assigns Craig the evidentiary burden.

components.text: The affirmative must warrant its claimed probability increase with recognizable evidence rather than merely define it.

response.rationale: The move contacts the cumulative standard by challenging whether the affirmative has supplied evidence capable of satisfying it, while also assigning the burden of proof.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contests burden satisfaction, though it does not separately evaluate each affirmative consideration.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden claim is clear, but recognizable empirical evidence sometimes narrows evidence toward scientific evidence without a stable boundary.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Assigning the affirmative the burden to establish the motion is appropriate, subject to an implicit allowance for warranted nonexperimental evidence.

charity.alternative: The affirmative offers philosophical, moral, historical, and scientific evidence under a probability-raising standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such material still requires defended warrants and discrimination from alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The burden allocation is sound, though the inference from affirmative burden to an exclusively empirical standard is not fully defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden principle is defensible, but the preferred evidentiary boundary is asserted without a developed account of historical or philosophical warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the negative motion-level claim that the affirmative must supply warranted evidence favoring God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes an evidentiary claim but tends to narrow acceptable evidence toward the empirical and scientific categories.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss repeatedly states that Craig bears the onus to demonstrate evidence and that Krauss need not disprove God.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: An infinitely powerful divine intelligence is an extraordinary claim requiring correspondingly extraordinary evidence, which ordinary probability assertions do not by themselves supply.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss develops an explicit evidentiary criterion, illustrates what miraculous evidence might look like, and applies it to Craig's case.

components.text: A probability-raising definition does not alone show that the offered facts adequately warrant an extraordinary divine hypothesis.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the sufficiency of Craig's stated evidentiary standard by requiring stronger discrimination for an extraordinarily powerful intelligence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the standard's sufficiency but leaves the exact probabilistic basis for the heightened threshold underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The extraordinary-claim standard and its application to divine intelligence are clear, though its quantitative meaning remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A stronger warrant demand is defensible, but the move does not derive how much stronger evidence the divine hypothesis requires.

charity.alternative: Ordinary evidence can rationally raise the probability of an extraordinary hypothesis through cumulative likelihood ratios.
charity.decisiveQualification: The cumulative likelihoods and prior-sensitive comparison still must be defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidentiary demand is coherent, with a material missing bridge between extraordinariness and the precise required evidential threshold.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Illustrative miraculous evidence is discussed, but no representative probability analysis or general threshold defense is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary empirical-warrant requirement, though it does not independently complete the negative motion route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly challenges mere probability assertions but does not fully engage how multiple ordinary facts could accumulate evidential force.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts scientific evidentiary practice with Craig's formulation and identifies divine creative intelligence as an extraordinary claim.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Classical intuitions about the absurdity of infinity cannot override mathematics and empirically successful physics, both of which consistently employ infinite quantities.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss sustains the same rebuttal through methodological claims, a quantum-mechanical illustration, and a direct discussion of mathematical infinities.

components.text: The philosophical case against an infinite past cannot rest on classical absurdity intuitions when mathematics and physics successfully use infinities.

response.rationale: The move contacts one stated support for the beginning premise by disputing the inference from counterintuitive infinity examples to physical impossibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it reaches a decisive premise-support component but does not answer the separate scientific beginning evidence or causal inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clear, but mathematical infinities, divergent quantities, and an actually infinite temporal past are treated too interchangeably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Successful mathematical treatment of infinities does not by itself establish the physical possibility of an actually infinite past.

charity.alternative: The affirmative objection concerns an actually instantiated temporal infinity, not merely mathematical infinite series.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mathematical consistency does not settle metaphysical or physical instantiation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The methodological warning has force, but the inference equivocates between mathematical tools and the physical realization at issue.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete examples from complex analysis and physics are supplied, yet they do not verify an eternal physical past.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks a material support for the affirmative central cosmological-ground bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially weakens the affirmative distinction by relying on successful uses of mathematical infinity as if they resolved actual temporal infinity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss cites complex variables, infinite series, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics as successful domains employing infinity.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Contingency and presently unexplained causal processes do not support God, because unknown explanations invite investigation and may ultimately prove entirely physical.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss explicitly turns to Craig's first listed consideration and develops a continuous objection centered on accidents and unknown physical causes.

components.text: Presently unknown physical explanations do not license an inference from contingency to God.

response.rationale: The move attacks the contingency inference by characterizing it as substituting God for incomplete causal knowledge and urging continued physical investigation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the divine-identification gap but does not directly rebut the principle requiring an ultimate explanation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The no-gap principle is clear, but the move shifts from cosmic contingency to processes producing human beings, changing the argument's scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The prospect of physical explanation supports caution, though it does not itself answer the metaphysical contingency premise.

charity.alternative: The contingency argument concerns why any contingent reality exists, not an unexplained step in biological history.
charity.decisiveQualification: A physical process may explain an event while leaving the existence of contingent physical reality unexplained.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The caution against gap inferences is coherent, but its application partly misses the argument's ultimate-explanation premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical success of physical inquiry is invoked generally, without evidence that such inquiry supplies a necessary terminus.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the divine-identification step of the central cosmological bridge, albeit without defeating the entire contingency argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: By recasting the argument as ignorance about human origins, the move omits the strongest metaphysical scope of the contingency demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt labels the inference a God-of-the-gaps move and predicts that unknown causes may be discovered to be physical.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Quantum gravity, inflation, and a potentially eternal multiverse provide natural models in which our universe can arise spontaneously without a relevant divine first cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Krauss turn is identified by the moderator's transition to Craig at events 953 through 955.

components.text: An eternal inflationary multiverse would block the inference from our universe's beginning to a relevant divine first cause.

response.rationale: The move directly supplies a natural cosmological alternative under which our universe arises spontaneously from an eternal wider structure.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the divine first-cause inference but does not establish that the proposed multiverse is actually past eternal.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between our universe and an eternal multiverse is stable, and uncertainty about the multiverse's cause is acknowledged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately presents the multiverse as a physically motivated possibility rather than as an established cosmological fact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative coherently blocks a cause of our local universe from being an ultimate divine cause, conditional on past eternality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Inflation is specifically invoked as motivation, but the claim that the multiverse is past eternal is not established in the span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the negative natural-cosmology bridge by offering a direct alternative to a divine first cause.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a positive alternative without materially distorting the affirmative causal argument it is intended to block.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes inflation, an eternal multiverse, and spontaneous local-universe formation while acknowledging uncertainty about ultimate cause.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: If an act would remain wrong despite divine approval, moral truth constrains God's choices and therefore neither originates in God nor gains explanatory grounding from God.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Krauss's uninterrupted opening turn immediately before the moderator introduces Craig's rebuttal.

components.text: If moral wrongness constrains what God could approve, objective morality is not explained by divine choice.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the grounding inference: moral truth either remains independent of divine choice or divine approval could make grave acts permissible.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly identifies the disputed dependence inference and states why divine choice does not ground morality.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterfactual divine-approval test and the conclusion about moral independence are clearly and consistently expressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As a dilemma against morality based on unconstrained divine choice, the asserted consequence follows at the stated force.

charity.alternative: Morality may be grounded in God's necessary good nature rather than arbitrary divine choices.
charity.decisiveQualification: A nature-based account avoids voluntarist arbitrariness but must explain why that nature constitutes goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dilemma is clear and valid against choice-based morality, with a bounded gap concerning necessary divine-character accounts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The counterexample supplies a strong conceptual test, though no further defense addresses nature-based divine grounding.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable claim that objective moral truth obtains its ontology from God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly defeats simple divine voluntarism but omits the strongest necessary-nature version of divine grounding.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss asks whether divine approval could make rape permissible and infers that a negative answer makes morality independent of God's choice.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Mathematical treatments of infinity and quantum-vacuum cosmology do not defeat the evidence that the universe and its physical state began.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a continuous section of Craig's moderator-introduced rebuttal, with Krauss not resuming until events 1241 through 1242.

components.text: Quantum-vacuum and inflationary cosmologies do not establish a past-eternal physical state.
Mathematical manipulation of infinity does not show that an actual infinite temporal history exists.

response.rationale: The response contacts both the eternal-natural-model proposal and the appeal to mathematical infinity, invoking a boundary theorem against past eternality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly addresses the decisive past-eternality premise, though the theorem's assumptions are not examined in detail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The physical-state beginning claim is clear, but applicability conditions for the cited cosmological theorem remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The quoted proof rhetoric overstates what a theorem conditional on average expansion establishes about every quantum-gravity model.

charity.alternative: Some quantum-gravity or emergent models may evade the assumptions of the cited past-incompleteness theorem.
charity.decisiveQualification: Past incompleteness is not identical to an absolute beginning from nothing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rebuttal targets the correct premise, but it compresses the inference from theorem-based incompleteness to an absolute cosmic beginning.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A named theorem and an author quotation provide specific support, with a material gap about assumptions and interpretive scope.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the negative central natural-cosmology bridge by denying that its wider physical state can be eternal.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response addresses past eternality forcefully but omits the decisive distinction between geodesic incompleteness and creation from nothing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig invokes the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem and quotes Vilenkin as requiring cosmologists to face a cosmic beginning.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Quantum-gravitational origins, universes with varying laws, and observer selection provide physical explanations for apparent fine-tuning without supernatural imposition.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Krauss's uninterrupted response turn, explicitly bounded by moderator transitions at events 1241 and 1572 through 1574.

components.text: Physical processes, varied laws, and observer selection can account for apparent fine-tuning without supernatural design.

response.rationale: The move directly contests the design inference by supplying physical-generation and selection mechanisms as alternative sources of apparent fine-tuning.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the decisive design-versus-natural-alternatives comparison, though the proposed cosmology remains incompletely specified.

precisionFindings.rationale: The natural-alternative claim is recoverable, but biological selection and cosmological observer selection are analogized somewhat loosely.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers natural mechanisms as live alternatives and generally preserves uncertainty about unresolved quantum-gravity details.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative-explanation strategy is coherent, with one material bridge from biological analogy to cosmological fine-tuning.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several specific physical mechanisms are identified, but their probability distributions and capacity to generate life-permitting domains are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central negative bridge requiring physical alternatives and observer selection to undercut design.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response proposes positive physical alternatives without depending on a material caricature of the affirmative design inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage invokes quantum-gravitational origins, varying laws, observer environments, and natural selection as ways apparent design can arise physically.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A many-worlds hypothesis does not explain embodied interactive observers and instead relocates fine-tuning to the laws governing the multiverse.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn continues Craig's rebuttal, explicitly addresses Krauss by name, and ends before Craig changes to morality.

components.text: A multiverse must explain embodied observers and the special laws governing universe production rather than merely multiply worlds.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges whether the proposed many-worlds mechanism has explanatory scope and argues that it relocates rather than removes fine-tuning.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the alternative's decisive explanatory claim and identifies two concrete residual demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The observer and higher-level-law objections are clearly separated, though the relevant measure problem is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The objections expose genuine gaps, but saying many worlds does nothing overlooks possible observer-selection explanatory force.

charity.alternative: A sufficiently varied multiverse plus observer selection can explain why observers find life-permitting conditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The generating laws and measure still require justification and may themselves be special.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress-to-generating-laws objection is coherent, with a bounded overstatement concerning the explanatory contribution of selection effects.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explanatory deficits are specifically identified, but no evidence establishes that every viable multiverse generator must be comparably fine-tuned.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the negative central fine-tuning-alternatives bridge at its observer-selection and multiverse-law components.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the multiverse proposal's intended function and presses a legitimate higher-level qualification, though its initial dismissal is broad.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that many worlds do not explain embodied interactive observers and asks what determines the multiverse's special laws.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Divine commands necessarily express God's compassionate, just, and fair character, while naturalism lacks a foundation for objective moral duties and values.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly presents his divine-command account in a continuous turn and contrasts it with the moral implications he attributes to Krauss.

components.text: Necessary expressions of God's essentially compassionate and just character prevent arbitrary immoral commands.

response.rationale: The response contacts the arbitrariness horn by replacing unconstrained divine choice with commands necessarily expressing an essentially good character.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly answers the arbitrary-command challenge, though it does not fully explain why God's character constitutes goodness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The necessary-character account and its contrast with arbitrary commands are explicit and consistently scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Necessary divine character blocks voluntarist arbitrariness, but it does not alone establish unique ontological grounding.

charity.alternative: Moral standards may still assess God's character rather than derive their authority from it.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must explain constitution of goodness without circularly listing good traits.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modified divine-command account is coherent, with a material unresolved bridge between possessing good traits and grounding goodness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual response is specific, but the asserted essential properties and their unique grounding role receive little independent support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the negative secular-morality bridge by answering the central divine-arbitrariness objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly handles arbitrary divine commands but omits the strongest independence challenge directed at God's character itself.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that commands necessarily express God's compassionate, kind, just, and fair essence, excluding worlds with reversed moral commands.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Rationality, evolution, biology, and continued investigation can explain moral understanding and conduct without belief in or dependence upon God.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss continues his uninterrupted rebuttal, first rejecting the divine inference and then explicitly developing a naturalistic approach to morality.

components.text: Moral understanding and conduct can arise through rationality, evolution, and biology without belief in God.
Atheists' continued moral conduct challenges the claim that morality depends practically on belief in God.

response.rationale: The move contacts a naturalistic account of moral understanding but does not fully answer the affirmative's ontological claim about objective moral truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it supplies an epistemic and motivational alternative while leaving the decisive grounding question substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic thesis is clear, but understanding, motivation, conduct, and ontological grounding are not consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Krauss explicitly admits that biology and rationality may not completely define morality, matching the limited support offered.

charity.alternative: The affirmative argues about the ontology of objective values, not whether atheists can know or obey moral norms.
charity.decisiveQualification: An epistemic naturalistic account does not by itself provide a secular moral ontology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The naturalistic account coherently addresses moral cognition and behavior, but it does not entail an account of objective truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Common moral conduct and named biological and rational mechanisms provide support, though no developed moral theory is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the central secular-morality bridge, but only its understanding and conduct components rather than full ontology.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response partly substitutes moral knowledge and conduct for the stronger affirmative claim about objective moral grounding.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss observes that nonbelievers remain moral and identifies rationality, evolution, biology, and continued research as explanatory resources.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Known dynamics explain some alleged fine-tuning, while the unexplained vacuum-energy value is not shown to be life-necessary and does not evidence competent purposive design.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss explicitly announces his return to fine-tuning, discusses entropy and vacuum energy, and concludes the argument before the moderator opens summaries.

components.text: Known dynamics explain some alleged tuning, and the remaining vacuum-energy value is not shown to be intentionally life-directed.
Residual ignorance about a value does not establish design or purposeful multiverse laws.

response.rationale: The move answers the design comparison by distinguishing dynamically explained cases from unresolved values and by challenging the inference to competent purpose.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the core purposive-design inference, though some broad no-purpose language exceeds the narrower evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The specific fine-tuning objections are recoverable, but the conclusion expands from selected values to all cosmic purpose.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Acknowledged ignorance fits the local vacuum-energy claim, but the categorical assertion of no purpose or design exceeds that warrant.

charity.alternative: Life-permitting conditions may evidence design even if the resulting universe is inefficient or mostly hostile.
charity.decisiveQualification: Purpose need not imply maximal habitability, but alleged design must still predict the observed distribution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The local underdetermination argument is coherent, while the transition from poor apparent efficiency to no purpose is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Entropy and vacuum energy provide specific cases, but the universal no-design conclusion lacks representative comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central negative fine-tuning bridge by contesting both tuning and purposive interpretation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The incompetence objection is relevant but assumes a stronger optimal-design expectation than the affirmative expressly established.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss distinguishes dynamically explained entropy from unexplained vacuum energy and argues that the observed result poorly fits competent design.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Reports of Jesus's resurrection are more plausibly attributable to mistaken human testimony than to a miraculous event and therefore do not provide adequate evidence for God.
moves.attributionBasis: Krauss begins his announced summary, answers Craig's five points in sequence, and ends with thanks immediately before the moderator addresses the audience.

components.text: Anecdotal historical testimony is more likely to contain human error than to establish a miraculous resurrection.

response.rationale: The response contacts the evidentiary status of the resurrection reports by offering ordinary testimonial error as a more probable explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the testimony warrant but does not separately analyze the empty tomb, appearances, or transformed belief.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative testimonial-error claim is clear, though the category anecdotal does not specify the sources or dependence structure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ordinary error has a plausible base-rate advantage, but the move does not compare that advantage against each alleged historical fact.

charity.alternative: The affirmative relies on a conjunction of an empty tomb, appearances, and transformed belief rather than a single anecdote.
charity.decisiveQualification: The independence and historical establishment of those claims remain disputed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The base-rate comparison is coherent, with a material missing bridge connecting generic human error to the full fact set.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The ordinary-error alternative is plausible but is asserted generally without source-specific evidence or a detailed rival reconstruction.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the ordinary-historical-explanation bridge by challenging the reliability of the resurrection reports.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies a serious ordinary rival but compresses the affirmative's multi-fact comparative structure into anecdotal testimony.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span expressly characterizes the historical evidence as anecdotal and contrasts human testimonial error with miracle claims.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Human error, imagination, illusion, or deliberate intervention are more plausible explanations of resurrection claims than an extraordinary supernatural resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows a question directed to Krauss and uses his first-person comparisons with alien-abduction reports and physical plausibility.

components.text: Imagination, illusion, or deliberate intervention are ordinary explanations more plausible than supernatural resurrection.
The proposed ordinary rivals must account for the affirmative's complete three-fact set.

response.rationale: The move supplies several ordinary rival classes and explains their prior plausibility, but it does not show how any one rival explains all three alleged facts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it reaches the decisive comparative-explanation demand while leaving explanatory scope and detailed fit incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rival categories and comparative claim are clear, and the speaker explicitly avoids claiming that one has been established.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately limited to ordinary rivals being simpler and more plausible, without asserting a proven reconstruction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative base-rate reasoning is coherent, though no single alternative is shown to explain the entire alleged evidence set.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several familiar human mechanisms are specified, but no source-specific evidence establishes their operation in this historical case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central negative bridge requiring ordinary explanations to remain more plausible than resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response advances multiple ordinary alternatives and expressly acknowledges their unproven status without a material caricature.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss identifies imagination, illusion, and intentional intervention as simpler explanations while disclaiming proof of any particular one.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Widely accepted historical facts surrounding Jesus are best explained by resurrection because rival naturalistic accounts fail standard explanatory criteria.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker handoff names Craig, and the response reprises his specific historical case and scholarly explanatory criteria.

components.text: Naturalistic rivals fail explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and non-ad-hocness when applied to the accepted historical facts.
Generic testimonial error does not furnish a specific explanation with adequate scope for the cited facts.

response.rationale: The response directly compares the named ordinary theories against standard historical explanatory criteria and denies that generic error explains the full set.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the rival-explanation demand and states the criteria on which the proposed rivals allegedly fail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rival theories and explanatory criteria are stable, though the extent of scholarly rejection and fact acceptance is compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Comparative criteria are appropriate, but categorical failure of every naturalistic account is asserted without case-by-case demonstration.

charity.alternative: Different ordinary mechanisms may jointly explain different elements rather than one theory explaining every claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Composite explanations can lose simplicity but are not excluded merely by lacking a single mechanism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive comparison is well structured, with a bounded gap because the criteria are announced rather than applied in detail.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named rivals and standard criteria provide specific support, but scholarly adherence substitutes partly for demonstrated comparative analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central negative ordinary-history bridge and reinforces the affirmative resurrection explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move names major rivals fairly but evaluates them collectively and omits the strongest composite-error interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig names conspiracy, apparent-death, and hallucination theories and evaluates them using explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and ad hocness.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Explanatory inquiry stops non-arbitrarily with God because contingent things require external causes whereas God exists necessarily by his own nature.
moves.attributionBasis: The explicit rebuttal transition and the defense of the principle of sufficient reason identify Craig and his established contingency argument.

components.text: Stopping with a necessary being is principled because only contingent entities require external causes.
A merely eternal multiverse does not thereby possess necessity in its own nature.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the arbitrariness and regress objections by restating the necessary-versus-contingent explanatory principle and applying it to God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the decisive terminus objection, though it does not independently demonstrate that God has necessary existence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Necessary existence and contingent external causation are expressly distinguished and consistently applied to explanatory termination.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional terminus principle is clear, but asserting God's necessary nature does not by itself demonstrate that modal status.

charity.alternative: A natural structure rather than God might exist necessarily and terminate explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Eternal duration alone is not metaphysical necessity, but a natural necessitarian account remains possible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stopping rule is coherent and non-arbitrary conditional on necessary divine existence, which remains the material unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The principle is explicitly restated, but no independent modal argument establishes that God rather than a natural entity is necessary.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the negative natural-cosmology bridge and defends the affirmative necessary-ground completion condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response correctly distinguishes eternality from necessity while leaving the strongest necessary-natural-terminus alternative open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that every entity is explained by its own necessary nature or an external cause and places God in the first category.

moves.speaker: Lawrence Krauss
moves.proposition: Defining God as the necessary explanatory terminus has no demonstrated advantage over an eternal multiverse, which can serve as a natural terminus and is physically motivated.
moves.attributionBasis: The rebuttal handoff follows Craig's answer, and the speaker contrasts Craig's definition with Krauss's own physics-based multiverse proposal.

components.text: Defining God as necessary has no shown advantage over treating a physically motivated eternal multiverse as the terminus.
The affirmative must justify why the necessary explanation is divine rather than natural.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the asymmetry between divine and natural termini and offers the multiverse as a competing explanatory endpoint.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the identification gap but conflates eternal existence with metaphysical necessity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative challenge is clear, but eternal, necessary, and required for our universe are treated as interchangeable statuses.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A natural terminus is a live alternative, though physical motivation does not establish its necessity or past eternality.

charity.alternative: The affirmative distinguishes a metaphysically necessary being from an entity that merely has no temporal beginning.
charity.decisiveQualification: The divine necessity claim itself still requires justification and comparison with natural necessity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity objection is relevant, but defining the multiverse as eternal does not logically give it necessary existence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Physical motivation is asserted as an advantage, while no specific theory establishes the multiverse as an explanatory necessary terminus.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central negative natural-cosmology bridge by proposing a natural alternative terminus.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the comparative burden but materially blurs the affirmative's central necessity-versus-eternity distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Krauss explicitly parallels Craig's definition with an always-existing multiverse and claims his alternative is motivated by physics.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Restricting rational evidence to scientific proof is self-defeating, while theism jointly explains moral, philosophical, historical, and scientific facts.
moves.attributionBasis: The rebuttal transition and direct discussion of Krauss's epistemology clearly mark Craig's response to the preceding answer.

components.text: The legitimate demand is rationally warranted evidence, not an exclusive restriction to scientific proof.
A broad cumulative case can include moral, philosophical, historical, and scientific considerations while still requiring adequate warrants.
Theism's claimed advantage must be assessed across the full explanatory range rather than cosmology alone.

response.rationale: The reply justifies a broader evidentiary demand by arguing that scientism is self-defeating and then preserves warrant assessment across several evidence types.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it expressly replaces an overly narrow scientific criterion while retaining the legitimate requirement of explanatory evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Scientific, moral, philosophical, metaphysical, and historical evidence are clearly distinguished within a broad evidentiary category.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The critique of exclusive scientific proof is well fitted, but calling the God hypothesis powerful across all domains needs more comparative support.

charity.alternative: The negative may prioritize empirical testing without claiming that science is the only source of rational knowledge.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting strict scientism does not by itself validate every philosophical or historical inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-defeat objection and broader taxonomy are coherent, with a bounded bridge from admissibility to theism's explanatory success.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple evidence classes are specifically identified, but the span asserts rather than demonstrates their joint comparative support for theism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the negative motion-level evidentiary restriction and reconnects the affirmative cumulative case to the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly broadens evidence but partly treats Krauss's emphasis on empirical warrant as an exclusive scientistic doctrine.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig calls an exclusively scientific epistemology self-defeating and enumerates moral, philosophical, metaphysical, historical, and scientific evidence.
